topStories.headline: After a Decade of Delays, the Divisadero Car Wash Is Finally Getting Torn Down — and 203 Apartments Built in Its Place
topStories.dek: National developer Greystar has taken over the long-stalled NoPa/Lower Haight site and listed October 19 as its construction start date.
topStories.body:
<cite index="38-1">San Francisco's most notorious car wash is finally getting a new life as housing, with Greystar poised to take over the long-delayed Divisadero Street project and break ground on an eight-story, 203-unit apartment building.</cite> The shuttered Touchless Car Wash at 400 Divisadero — a fixture of NoPa frustration for years — became a symbol of the city's stalled housing pipeline after original plans were proposed back in 2015 and approvals were secured in 2025.

<cite index="38-3">The South Carolina-based apartment giant, which owns more than 110,000 units nationwide, is under contract to acquire the former Touchless Car Wash site and has lined up financing for construction, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.</cite> <cite index="38-4">Public Works permits allow the developer to close sidewalks and occupy part of an Oak Street traffic lane, with an October 19 construction start date listed.</cite> <cite index="38-8">A demolition permit for the car wash is still awaiting final approval.</cite>

<cite index="38-9">The project, originally shepherded by 4Terra Investments, includes 20 affordable apartments, roughly 1,850 square feet of retail, 24 parking spaces, and 144 bike-storage spots.</cite> <cite index="37-3">Greystar plans to invest in the property, taking responsibility for its development away from 4Terra Investments, which had already completed much of the design and permitting phase for the project.</cite>

<cite index="30-10,30-11">Just 405 housing units have been completed in San Francisco in 2026, the vast majority of them affordable. The city's state-mandated housing goals call for planning 82,000 units between 2023 and 2031.</cite> The Divisadero project would be among the first significant market-rate construction starts in the city this year. <cite index="42-7">With Greystar stepping in to fund the next phase, the site is closer than it has been in years to delivering 203 new homes — including 20 affordable units — in one of the city's most walkable, transit-connected neighborhoods.</cite>

topStories.headline: Hayes Valley's Entertainment Zone Is Up and Running — but a Dispute Over Who Controls the Street Isn't Going Away
topStories.dek: The EZ is open every Friday and Saturday, bringing to-go drinks and a farmers' market to the 400 block of Hayes, even as a neighborhood advocacy group keeps filing complaints about vendor permits and governance.
topStories.body:
<cite index="50-3,50-4">The Hayes Promenade, the Hayes Valley Merchants Council, and the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association launched the Hayes Valley Entertainment Zone, a designated area where to-go alcoholic drinks are permitted outside.</cite> <cite index="50-7">The EZ runs every Friday from 4pm to 10pm and Saturday from noon to 10pm, allowing people 21 and older to buy to-go cocktails, beer, and wine from participating businesses.</cite> <cite index="1-1">Hayes Street is also closed every Friday and Saturday for the companion Shared Spaces event.</cite>

Alongside the EZ, <cite index="65-3,65-4">starting June 6, 2026, the Hayes Valley Merchants Council, in cooperation with the Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association and the Hayes Promenade, brought the Pacific Coast Farmers' Market Association to the neighborhood. The new Saturday market operates weekly from 10:00 AM to 2:00 PM on the 400 block of Hayes Street.</cite>

Not everyone is celebrating. <cite index="47-1,47-2">Hayes Valley Safe, a community advocacy organization, has sent correspondence throughout 2024 and again in January 2025, August 2025, September 2025, January 2026, March 2026, June 2026, and August 2026, documenting continued vendor activity, recurring permit compliance concerns, and the absence of visible enforcement.</cite> <cite index="47-8">The group notes that the Hayes Valley Entertainment Zone has now entered its implementation phase.</cite>

<cite index="47-11,47-12">When Hayes Valley was added to San Francisco's Entertainment Zone ordinance in June 2025, many residents and independent businesses learned of the proposal only after it was already advancing through the legislative process. Throughout the following year, Hayes Valley Safe participated extensively in the review process through correspondence and review.</cite> The management plan was published by the city in July 2026. For now, the EZ continues operating each weekend while the governance questions remain unresolved.
topStories.sourceName: Hayes Valley Safe / Explore Hayes Valley

topStories.headline: D5 Supervisor Race Heats Up with November Vote Six Weeks Out: Four Candidates, Multiple Forums
topStories.dek: With the District 5 seat on the November 3 ballot, candidates Vallie Brown, Ryan Lam, Nomvula O'Meara, and Dean Preston are appearing at a series of public forums — including one at the SF Main Library this week.
topStories.body:
<cite index="80-1,80-3">Five of the eleven seats on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors are up for election, with three seats scheduled to be decided in the November 3, 2026 general election.</cite> District 5 — which includes Hayes Valley, Alamo Square, NoPa, Haight-Ashbury, Fillmore, and the Western Addition — is among them.

<cite index="56-1">The four candidates in the race are Vallie Brown, Ryan Lam, Nomvula O'Meara, and Dean Preston.</cite> <cite index="56-4">The League of Women Voters of San Francisco, together with co-sponsors D5 Action, the Haight Ashbury Neighborhood Council, and the Junior League of San Francisco, has organized forums for the candidates.</cite> <cite index="56-10">Doors open at 5:30pm for at least one upcoming forum.</cite>

The Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association's calendar lists a D5 Supervisor Candidate Forum at the SF Public Library this Friday, September 25. The UCSF Events Calendar confirms the same set of four candidates. <cite index="56-20,56-21,56-22">For each San Francisco election, the League of Women Voters of San Francisco organizes and co-sponsors moderated non-partisan forums for candidates to present their views on the issues most important to voters. The League does not support or oppose candidates or political parties. The events are non-partisan, free, and open to the public.</cite>

<cite index="56-15">District 5 includes the Inner Sunset, Haight-Ashbury, Cole Valley, Lower Haight, Hayes Valley, Alamo Square, Fillmore/Western Addition, Japantown, Cathedral Hill, and Lower Pacific Heights.</cite> <cite index="56-9">Audience members will be asked to submit non-partisan written questions.</cite>
topStories.sourceName: UCSF Events Calendar / Hayes Valley Neighborhood Association

moreNews.headline: 650 Divisadero Affordable Housing Project Awaiting Final Building Permits as Fall Construction Window Approaches
moreNews.body: <cite index="93-2,93-3">Plans have been approved for a ten-story apartment complex at 650 Divisadero Street. The proposal will add over a hundred units of affordable housing to a corner lot along Grove Street, a block away from Alamo Square and just a few blocks from the Golden Gate Park Panhandle.</cite> <cite index="96-1,96-2,96-3">Developers received approved entitlements from the city's planning department in mid-June. New building permits were requested in August and are still listed as under review. Construction is estimated to cost around $101 million.</cite> <cite index="98-2">Construction is slated for Fall 2026, with over $21 million in city funding.</cite> <cite index="93-4,93-5,93-6,93-7">The Young Community Developer and Jonathan Rose Companies are jointly sponsoring the project in partnership with MOHCD. The 98-foot-tall structure is expected to produce 107 apartments across 105,900 square feet, with unit types ranging from 27 studios to 27 three-bedrooms.</cite>
